newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Pacific Lithium on verge of breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Pacific Lithium on verge of breakthrough.

text.p: New Zealand's Pacific Lithium Ltd is one step away from cracking technology that could finally bring the cost of lithium batteries down by "farming" the mineral where it is most prevalent -- the sea.

Pacific Lithium Ld (PLL) Managing Director Robin Johannink said lithium is widely believed to be one of the most important strategic minerals of the future as battery technology advances in leaps and bounds.
But at present, 96 percent of the world's supply is controlled by just two players, FMC and Cyprus Amax, something that worries existing and potential users.

"There is a general vulnerability to users of lithium at the moment, especially in the expanding industries like batteries, when you've basically only got two suppliers in the world," Johannink told Reuters in a recent interview.
Johannink said PLL had developed a matrix, or powder, that absorbs lithium from the sea and from geothermal water.
The problem now is that the matrix needs to be put into a coating, or binder, that will absorb lithium but stop the matrix from dispersing.
Binders used so far have only acted to inhibit the process.
"The challenge now is in developing the best products that will interact with the matrix we've developed so that we can get as close as possible to a perfect uptake," he said.
"We've gone through 8,000 recipes alone to try and develop the optimum form and we are still not there. But we know 7,999 that don't work very well."
PLL's efforts to date have attracted the interest of giant Japanese trading house, Nissho Iwai Corp, which recently invested 200 million yen for a small stake.
Vertex Asia Group, part of the Singapore Government-owned Singapore Technologies, also has a holding.
PLL plans to build a refinery on the west coast of the Firth of Thames, to the south east of Auckland, and to operate a sea farm there.
Lithium comes from rock mining, but miners now are increasingly becoming involved in brine mining in the dried-up geothermal lakes of South America's Andes.
From there, lithium carbonate is formed to create the energy storage part of a lithium battery, which has a longevity advantage over nickel cadmium batteries.
PLL plans to extract lithium using a series of tapes suspended in water in the middle of the Firth of Thames.
The tapes are molecularly porous with each hole the size of a lithium molecule, which is the third down the line in the periodic table after hydrogen and helium.
The hydrogen and helium pass through the holes but lithium gets stuck. Bigger molecules can not pass through.
After passively absorbing lithium, the tapes will be taken back to PLL's plant at Wharekawa and put in a bath.

The lithium is then "sprung off" into light acid solution and electrolytically driven through a membrane to become lithium hydroxide. Carbon dioxide is added as the reactor, producing lithium carbonate.
Johannink said the project had a theoretical capacity of 4,000 tonnes a year, extracting lithium from the one billion cubic tonnes of water that surges through the area every hour.
From there PLL plans to joint-venture the technology.
PLL expects to start lithium processing in March next year, having just a just secured a contract to buy lithium hydroxide for conversion to lithium carbonate.
The exercise would test out PLL's land-based systems and give the company some general trading experience before its sea operations come on stream.
He expects PLL to be a cash flow business by next April, with profits to be ploughed back into research.
The world currently produces 50,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate, but PLL expects this to expand fourfold within five years as lithium batteries come to the fore.
PLL estimates that by 1998, 38 percent of all rechargeable batteries will be using lithium, up from four percent in 1994.
"Lithium batteries that are extremely powerful, 100 percent recyclable, non-toxic and light in weight will create a major leap forward for electric motor vehicles," Johannink said.
Lithium could be brought to the world cheaper.
"If we can pass on the beneifts of cheaper lithium, we are talking about very very quickly making electric motor vehicles viable for the world market."
